claims.claim: Vaccination gives the body a safe form of a germ so it builds protection without getting the disease; the CDC working definition states that vaccines help the body learn to defend itself from disease without the dangers of a full-blown infection.
Vaccines work by imitating an infection to engage the body's natural defenses; the active ingredient in a vaccine is an antigen, which causes the immune system to begin producing antibodies.
After the immune response is over, white blood cells stop multiplying, their numbers dwindle, and only a few remain to keep watch — this retained watch force is how the body remembers a germ.

Immunity is protection against a disease; a person who is immune is partially or fully resistant to the germ that causes it, and vaccine-induced immunity results from exposure to killed or weakened germs, or pieces of them, through vaccination.

Inactivated vaccines use a killed version of the germ; live-attenuated vaccines use a weakened form of the germ; mRNA vaccines give the body's cells instructions for making a protein (or piece of a protein) of the germ — and all vaccine types spark an immune response.

CDC notes non-live (inactivated-type) vaccines typically require three or more doses because their protection fades over time and must be restored with boosters, while live-attenuated vaccines can offer long-lasting protection with two doses and are not given to people with severely weakened immune systems.

The U.S. immunization program is organized around CDC-recommended schedules — one for children and adolescents (birth to 18) and one for adults (19 and older) — and CDC advises everyone to get recommended vaccines on schedule, including catch-up doses of missed vaccines.

In 2025, about 85 percent of infants worldwide (roughly 110 million children) received three doses of the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis vaccine, while 13.5 million children received no vaccine doses at all (WHO Immunization coverage fact sheet, 15 July 2026; data year 2025).

Vaccinated people can and sometimes do get infected after vaccination, but they are far less likely to die or become seriously ill than someone whose immune system is unprepared; immune protection is never perfect.
Vaccination heads CDC's list of the ten great public health achievements of the twentieth century, and WHO describes immunization as one of the most successful public health interventions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether vaccination prevents infection itself or mainly prevents serious disease.
positions: CDC: vaccinated people can and sometimes do get infected, but are far less likely to die or become seriously ill.
Popular accounts sometimes claim vaccination prevents infection entirely.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the CDC position: the recorded benefit is a large reduction in serious illness and death; infection remains possible, so protection is never perfect. No claim of guaranteed protection is made.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Herd-immunity thresholds are sometimes quoted as a single fixed population percentage.
positions: Some sources present one universal threshold figure.
CDC frames the needed level of group protection as varying by disease.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Out of scope by design: herd immunity is a sibling topic. This lesson names the concept only to point to the sibling topic and states no threshold.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft made no verifiable factual claims: its generic boilerplate ('Vaccination is a foundational concept in Public Health', 'College courses use vaccination as a building block', 'Think of vaccination as a label on a toolbox drawer') was discarded in full.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft boilerplate with a CDC-attributed working definition of vaccination.
Added the honest note (protection is never perfect; infection remains possible) so the lesson does not overclaim effectiveness.
Attributed the global coverage figures to WHO with their vintage (2025 data, reported July 2026).
Kept herd-immunity content out of scope and routed readers to the sibling topic instead.
No invented statistics: the only figures used are the WHO-reported coverage numbers, dated and attributed.
rightsIssues: None blocking. The CDC pages and the MMWR report are U.S. government works (public domain); MedlinePlus is a U.S. government source; the WHO fact sheet is reference-only, with facts restated in original prose and no reproduced wording.
